opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm fairly satisfied, maybe more than I expected a few years ago. The gap between a paper coming out and people actually using the idea has shrunk a lot. A few years back, a strong result might take a long time to show up in anything a normal person touches. Now, image generation is built into chat assistants, design tools, and phone apps, and people who have never read a paper use it every day.

That said, what reaches products is usually a filtered version of what's possible. Controllability is the main thing. Research has made real progress on consistent characters, precise editing, following long, compositional prompts, and getting text in images right, but in many products you still end up regenerating ten times to get what you wanted. The raw capability exists; the interfaces and reliability haven't fully caught up.

There's also a natural lag for good reasons: safety, cost, and latency. A method that looks great in a paper may be too expensive to serve to millions of users, or may need guardrails before it can be released. So some of that delay is just engineering maturity, not a failure.

Coming from the language side, I see the same pattern there. The most interesting thing now is less pure image generation and more multimodal models that reason across text and images together. That's where I think the next big product jump comes from, and where we still have a lot of work to do.

r001.rationale: The response says research advances reach phone apps, but products offer a filtered version and their interfaces and reliability lag behind the raw capability, leaving users to regenerate repeatedly.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say I'm fairly satisfied, more than I expected to be a few years ago. If you look at how fast things went from the first diffusion papers to tools people actually use every day, the gap between research and product has been remarkably short compared to other areas of machine learning. You have image generation in design tools, in phones, in ad creation, and most people using them have no idea what a latent diffusion model is, which is exactly how it should be.

That said, I think there are two places where I'm less satisfied. The first is that a lot of what ends up in products is the "pretty picture" use case, and that's only a small part of what the research enables. Things like controllable editing, consistency across frames, understanding spatial relationships, these are much harder and much more useful for real work, and they're still rough in most products. You can generate a stunning image in one shot, but ask for a precise change to a specific object and it often falls apart.

The second is that the ecosystem is still quite concentrated. A lot of the best capabilities sit behind a handful of APIs. Open models have been very important here, maybe more than in language, because the community built an enormous amount of tooling on top of them, LoRAs, ControlNets, all of that. I'd like to see more of that openness survive as the models get bigger and more expensive to train, because that's really what lets the long tail of products exist rather than just a few big ones.

So overall: impressive adoption, but I think we've captured the easy value and the deeper value is still mostly in the papers.

r001.rationale: The candidate says image generation has reached phones and everyday products quickly, but does not describe a gap between research demos and the speaker’s ability to use those advances on a phone today.

astra-6.text: I’m not completely satisfied. You see impressive progress in research, but that doesn’t always translate into something people can reliably use. Generating a beautiful image is one thing; getting precisely the image you had in mind, then changing one detail without changing everything else, is another. I’d like to see more of the advances show up as control and reliability in everyday products.

r001.rationale: The response identifies a gap between research progress and reliable use in everyday products, but it does not say whether the speaker can use those advances on a phone today.

sol-6.1.text: I have mixed feelings. It’s exciting that people can use image generation so easily now, but I think there’s still a gap between a compelling research demo and something you can reliably use every day. You can get a beautiful image very quickly, but getting exactly the image you intended, and then making a precise change while preserving everything else, can still be frustrating. So I’m excited by the progress, but I wouldn’t say we’re fully there yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between research demos and reliable everyday use, but does not mention using the advances on a phone.
